name: Uma Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Uma, thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any tech company, employer, union or party, and what you say stays confidential. Can you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior agent at Nest & Key, which is a small, quite young agency in the city centre that does sales and lettings for flats near the canal. My day starts with the AI assistant sorting overnight enquiries into hot, maybe and time-waster, then I ring the hot ones before nine. After that it's viewings, video tours for people moving from abroad, and a lot of messaging. I love the variety, and I love finding a shortcut that saves the team an hour.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, or what are you still finding hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Valuations. Ravi, our director, can walk into a flat and say two hundred and ten thousand, and he's right within a few grand. I'm still way off, and when a landlord pushes back I wobble. I'm great with the tools but the actual judgement part is where I'm weakest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd post something like: turns out AI is a really good intern, not a new boss. At work I'd keep showing people my little tricks, because even a plateau AI saves time on enquiries. I'd be honest that I'm a bit disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the boring bits stay a bit faster and the job stays the job. I'd have to get good at valuations the slow way, by watching Ravi. My savings are solid, I lived with my mum until I was 25 and banked most of my pay, so I'm not worried about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Nest & Key and ask Ravi to take me on every valuation for six months. I'd keep building small automations, like the enquiry sorting and the viewing reminders. I'd probably put some of my savings into a housing co-op share scheme my friend Jo is involved in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, like a film that had a great trailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put money into a housing co-op. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I think housing's broken and co-ops are one of the few fixes I believe in. My friend Jo lives in one by the old mill, and the rent is a third lower than what I let flats for. Working for an estate agency and investing in a housing co-op that would cut agents out feels a bit odd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world that would bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rents still going up every year and nothing changing. I'd still be showing a nurse a studio for half her pay. If AI was supposed to change things and it didn't, the same old problems just stay.

say: I'd post that AI turned out to be a **good intern**, not a new boss.
I'd keep sharing my **time-saving tricks** with the team at work.
think: The job stays the job, and I learn **valuations** the slow way.
My **savings** from living at home mean money isn't a worry.
do: **Shadow Ravi** on every valuation for six months.
Keep building small **automations** for enquiries and viewing reminders.
**Buy co-op shares** in the scheme my friend Jo belongs to.
S0.quote: Working for an estate agency and investing in a housing co-op that would cut agents out feels a bit odd.
fieldNote: She's openly **disappointed** AI didn't do more.
She names her weakness, **valuation judgement**, without being asked twice.
Her money goes toward a **housing co-op**, matching her politics.

steps.text: Shadow the director on every valuation for six months
Build automatic viewing reminders for the Nest & Key team
Buy shares in the old mill housing co-op

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment agencies decide whether AI makes jobs better or just cheaper. I'd be loud online about keeping people and cutting hours instead. At work I'd volunteer to run the change, because I'm already the one people ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is actually good for me. I'm already the person at Nest & Key who sets up the tools, so I'd become the one who runs them. The juniors who just book viewings would struggle, and I'd feel bad about that, but my own role would probably grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd pitch Ravi on making me the office's systems person, part agent, part tool runner, with a pay bump. I'd write simple how-to guides for everyone so nobody's left behind. I'd keep saving and keep the co-op shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly, with a bit of guilt. I'd enjoy it more than I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel guilty. About whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Benji, who started the same month as me. He's lovely with buyers but he still prints out his diary. If the office shrinks, Ravi keeps the one who can run the systems, and that's me, not Benji.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said the job could get better or cheaper. What would you do if Ravi chose cheaper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd argue with Ravi, properly, because he listens to me on this stuff. If he still cut people, I'd probably look elsewhere, there are loads of agencies in the city. I don't want to be the person who built the AI system that sacked my mates at the agency.

say: I'd say AI must make jobs **better**, not just **cheaper**.
I'd **volunteer** to run the change at my agency.
think: As the person who **sets up tools**, my role would likely grow.
Juniors who only **book viewings** would struggle, which worries me.
do: **Pitch Ravi** on a systems role with a **pay bump**.
**Write how-to guides** so no colleague is left behind.
Keep the **savings** and co-op shares as they are.
S1.quote: I don't want to be the person who built the AI system that sacked my mates at the agency.
fieldNote: She sees **opportunity** first and others' risk second.
Her **guilt** about colleague Benji is specific and unprompted.
She would **push back** on her director if gains went to cuts.

steps.text: Pitch a part-agent, part-systems role with a pay rise
Write simple tool guides for every Nest & Key colleague
Push the director to cut hours rather than staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need something like a universal basic income, fast, because this hits everyone at once. I'd be online a lot, and at work I'd say be honest with each other about what's coming. I'd stop pretending I've got it all figured out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the tools won't protect me. If AGI can value a flat better than our director Ravi by 2028, being good with tools doesn't save a junior agent like me. Viewings last until robots around 2031, but that's a key-holder job, not an agent job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to move sideways into housing co-ops or community land trusts, where they'll need people who understand both property and the tech. I'd offer to help the old mill co-op for free at first. My savings would let me take a pay cut for a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, a churning kind of feeling. But I'd rather be moving than frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'free at first'. How long could you afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe eight months if I'm careful, longer if I move into the co-op. I've worked it out on a spreadsheet before, just for fun. That's a very me thing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum not to worry because I saved like she taught me. She worked in a laundry for twenty years and she always said keep three months under the mattress. I've got more than that, so this is exactly what her advice was for.

say: I'd call for a **basic income** quickly, since it hits everyone.
I'd tell colleagues to be **honest** about what's coming.
think: Being good with tools **doesn't save** a junior agent from AGI.
Viewings until **2031** are a key-holder job, not an agent job.
do: **Move sideways** into housing co-ops or community land trusts.
**Volunteer** for the old mill co-op before asking for pay.
**Take a pay cut** for a year or two using savings.
S2.quote: If AGI can value a flat better than our director Ravi by 2028, being good with tools doesn't save a junior agent like me.
fieldNote: Her adaptability shows: she moves **toward housing co-ops**, not away from work.
She has already **costed** a pay cut on a spreadsheet.
Her **mum's laundry** job and saving advice shape her money habits.

steps.text: Volunteer with the old mill co-op to learn its work
Live on savings through a year of lower co-op pay
Join campaigns calling for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's design this properly, with basic income pilots and retraining paid by the companies making the money. I'd be organising, not just posting. At work I'd run workshops on the tools for other agencies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. Five years is long enough for me to build a second career in co-op housing and keep a hand in agency tech. I'd probably be more useful in 2031 than I am now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study a part-time housing management course from next year, paid from savings. I'd keep working at Nest & Key and get paid extra for helping other offices set up tools. I'd also put more into the co-op, maybe move in if a flat comes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy for my friends, mostly fine for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine. What part of it still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching agents like Benji wait too long. In five years you can learn anything, but only if you start. I'd be nagging Benji every month, and he'd hate me for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would moving into the co-op change your plans for a family or partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm single right now, so it's more about having a cheap, stable home. Co-op rent would let me take a lower wage for the work I care about. That's the whole point of a co-op, isn't it.

say: I'd push for **basic income pilots** funded by AI companies.
I'd **run workshops** on AI tools for other agencies.
think: Five years lets me build a **second career** in co-op housing.
I'd probably be **more useful** in 2031 than now.
do: **Study housing management** part-time from next year.
**Earn extra** helping other offices set up tools.
**Move into the co-op** if a flat comes up.
S3.quote: In five years you can learn anything, but only if you start.
fieldNote: Five years turns her risk into a **two-track career**.
Her concern centres on **colleagues who wait**, not herself.
A cheap **co-op home** is part of her money plan.

steps.text: Enrol in part-time housing management study from next year
Charge other agencies to set up their AI tools
Move into the old mill co-op when a flat opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make this fair, if we start now. I'd want rules on AI in housing decisions, like who gets a tenancy. I'd be campaigning and also helping agencies adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the comfortable one for me. I'd become the person who knows housing and knows the tech, and that's valuable for a long time. By 2036 I'd be 37 with ten years of experience in exactly the right mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Nest & Key and grow the systems side over the next three years. Then I'd move into a co-op or housing association in a tech role. I'd keep investing in the co-op and keep my savings strong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little excited. It feels like a path rather than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rules on who gets a tenancy. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the AI tool we use at the agency already scores tenants, and it marks down people with gaps in their work history. A human would ask why there's a gap. Ten years of that unchecked would be awful for people already struggling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that still worries you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people hear ten years and relax. It's the same end point, just later. I'd hate for my friends to wake up in 2035 with nothing planned.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to **make this fair**.
I'd campaign for **rules on AI** deciding tenancies.
think: Knowing **housing and tech** together stays valuable for years.
By **2036** I'd have the right mix of experience.
do: **Grow the systems side** at Nest & Key over three years.
Move into a **tech role** at a co-op or housing association.
S4.quote: The AI tool we use at the agency already scores tenants, and it marks down people with gaps in their work history. A human would ask why there's a gap.
fieldNote: She sees the long timeline as a **clear path** for herself.
Her strongest concern is **AI tenant scoring** that she has seen in use.
She worries friends will **relax** too much with ten years.

steps.text: Expand the systems side of the job at Nest & Key
Apply for tech roles at housing associations within three years
Keep adding to the co-op share holding
Campaign for rules on AI tenant scoring

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even I wouldn't have time, and my friends would be in a much worse place. What would help is a basic income or at least paid retraining, so people can move into the work that's left without panicking.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who decides who gets a home. Like I said, that scoring tool is already in our office. Agencies will use AI to sort people for homes, and nobody's checking it.

headlineQuote: Agencies will use AI to sort people for homes, and nobody's checking it.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old junior agent** at a young city-centre agency who uses AI tools every day.
She is fast with technology but still **weak on valuations**, and says so openly.
**Strong savings** from living with her mum let her plan a move into housing co-ops.
Her **progressive views** show in support for basic income, co-ops and rules on AI tenant scoring.
She stays **calm** in mild and slow scenarios and becomes anxious only when AGI arrives by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even she wouldn't have time to move.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or **paid retraining** so people can move without panic.
